author: Sally Rooney
en_title: Intermezzo: The People We Think We Know
zh_title: 《Intermezzo》：父亲去世之后，生活还在发生
en_deck: Two brothers lose the same father and enter different kinds of loneliness. Sally Rooney offers a reason to look again at the people we have already decided we understand.
zh_deck: 两个兄弟失去了同一个父亲，却没有共同的语言安放悲伤。Sally Rooney让我们再看一眼那些自以为已经了解的人。
en_notice: Introduces the initial relationships and a few early scenes, without revealing major turns or the ending. Discusses bereavement, chronic pain, medication, and adult sexual relationships.
zh_notice: 涉及人物的初始关系和少量早期情节，保留主要转折与结局。内容涉及丧亲、慢性疼痛、用药及成年人的亲密关系。人名沿用英文。
en_body:
Peter has a good deal to say about the suit his brother wore to their father's funeral. He can account for its ugliness, imagine where Ivan bought it, and fit the whole thing into a familiar picture of the younger man's indifference to appearances. Then Naomi asks how Ivan is doing. Peter admits that he has no idea.

That small failure of knowledge, in the [publisher's opening extract](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374602635/intermezzo/), makes an inviting entrance to Sally Rooney's fourth novel. Before asking what *Intermezzo* has to say about grief or love, we might stay with this brother: observant, articulate, affectionate in ways he cannot quite manage, and wrong to suppose that observation has brought him close.

You need not have read *Normal People*, or have settled an opinion about Rooney, to enter here. The immediate situation is easy enough to grasp. A father has died. His two adult sons are living through the aftermath, alongside three women whose lives are entangled with theirs. Knowing the relationships takes a moment. Understanding what anyone wants from them will take longer.

The interesting delay is between those two kinds of knowledge. We may have decided what a gesture means before the next paragraph lets us hear the hesitation behind it. Someone who seemed obvious a moment ago becomes troublesome again.

## Your brother has already been cast

Peter is thirty-two, a lawyer in Dublin. Ivan is twenty-two, a competitive chess player. One looks fluent in adult life; the other is visibly uncomfortable with much of it. A ten-year age gap gives each brother plenty of material for a misleading story.

This happens in families with a peculiar ease. The younger child remains the younger child long after he has grown up. The older one's confidence becomes evidence that he needs no help. Shared history can make an interpretation feel exempt from checking: I was there, I remember, I know what you're like. At some point, a description stops being information and starts assigning a part.

Peter's professional competence does not keep him steady after the funeral. The publisher's account tells us that he is taking medication to sleep. Ivan's chess ability, meanwhile, does not settle what kind of future he can expect. In her [interview with Cressida Leyshon](https://www.newyorker.com/books/this-week-in-fiction/sally-rooney-07-08-24), Rooney cautions against treating Ivan as an undiscovered world champion. He is talented; his talent does not promise that sort of destiny.

Neither intelligence nor a respectable occupation releases someone from the difficulty of living. That is easy to accept in the abstract and surprisingly hard to remember when a clever person we love makes a mess. Surely he should have worked this out. Surely, with his advantages, he could do better.

Bereavement gives the brothers a common event without giving them a common way of speaking. It is tempting to award maturity to the one who seems more composed, or sincerity to the one who seems less socially polished. The opening suggests that both verdicts would be premature. A person's manner is something we encounter. His grief is not necessarily available in it.

## Intimacy travels at different speeds

Peter is involved with Naomi, a university student, while remaining deeply attached to Sylvia, his former partner, whose life has been changed by an accident and chronic pain. Ivan meets Margaret, an older woman working at an arts centre, whose own marriage has become a source of difficulty. The relationships begin with histories already attached.

Peter and Naomi's first scene offers a particularly sharp detail. They are physically comfortable with each other; money passes between them; yet she has only just learned that his father has died. Their closeness has developed unevenly. Bodies, practical help, family news, and public recognition have reached different places.

It would be possible to read this merely as an indictment of Peter. But the scene makes room for a more uncomfortable question: how often do people find themselves living inside an arrangement they have never quite described? A private habit acquires rules. Certain questions remain unasked. One person treats a limit as obvious while the other has not agreed to it.

Naomi can answer back. Her jokes also make Peter's account of their relationship harder to sustain without embarrassment. Listening to her means noticing more than the effect she has on his mood. She has been managing days about which he knows little, just as he has been withholding news that would have mattered to her.

The publicly available [“Opening Theory”](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2024/07/08/opening-theory-fiction-sally-rooney) offers a different beginning. Margaret expects the visiting chess prodigy to be a child. Ivan arrives, unmistakably grown, and the encounter has already escaped her expectation before either of them has done much.

Ivan is attracted to her and anxious about mistaking professional friendliness for personal interest. His silence is busy. From outside, he might simply look awkward; from within, a brief pause contains an elaborate effort to avoid presuming too much.

There is something touching about that effort, and something recognisable. Being careful with another person can leave us unable to tell whether we are being considerate or retreating. Margaret has a job to do. Ivan would like the conversation to mean something beyond it. No amount of skill at chess will establish what her next response ought to mean.

The age differences invite comparison: an older man with a younger woman, a younger man with an older woman. Our reactions may not be symmetrical. Financial security, experience, and familiar gender expectations can influence what we call plausible, troubling, or romantic. The fact that everyone is an adult begins that discussion; it does not finish it.

## Before a thought becomes a sentence

One useful way to decide whether this book is for you is to compare the two available extracts. Peter's opening moves in short bursts, doubling back through impressions, judgments, and memories. “Opening Theory” gives hesitation a more patient unfolding. These are different reading rhythms, not simply two sets of biographical facts.

Peter's quickness may initially feel like an advantage. He has language for what he notices. Then the fragments start to reveal the strain of maintaining that assurance. We enter a mind already in motion, without a neat introduction to every change of direction. Understanding may arrive a beat after the sentence.

Ivan gives another kind of work to the reader. His attempts to understand a social exchange can linger over something another person would barely register. A pause in conversation becomes an event because of what might be misread inside it. The interest lies partly in watching him prepare an answer, then discover that preparing it has not made speaking easy.

Rosie Ofori Ward's [ABC review](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-10-01/intermezzo-sally-rooney-review/104413414) describes the contrast between Peter's fractured movement and Ivan's more deliberate thinking, and notes Margaret's separate perspective. Her response to the novel's slower pace is largely appreciative. Curtis Yee, in his [Associated Press review](https://apnews.com/article/7bd20450504ea13131f770a4bac9d33b), singles out Rooney's ability to catch feelings that have not yet become entirely legible to the people experiencing them.

Those accounts point to a pleasure visible in the extracts: the interval before somebody can give a feeling its name. We often talk as if emotions arrive with clear instructions. In ordinary life, we may know only that a conversation has unsettled us. Explanation comes afterward, sometimes in a form that is convenient rather than convincing.

Rooney's dialogue also goes without the conventional enclosure of quotation marks. Speech and inward thought sit close together. A reader who occasionally goes back to establish whether something was spoken has not necessarily lost the thread; identifying the shift is part of attending to the voice. It can help to read through a scene before returning to its smaller movements.

This is also a fair warning about pace. If you want a novel driven chiefly by escalating external events, try a few pages before committing. A conversation reconsidered can be gripping, but a taste for that kind of attention cannot be supplied by critical praise. The extracts let you make the decision in the company of Rooney's actual sentences.

## How much life does a supporting character get?

There is a second reason to keep the reviews close without allowing them to decide the reading. Their disagreements can sharpen a question.

Ward finds depth in the novel's slower movement, while also noticing how Sylvia and Naomi reach us through Peter's constricted view. In a substantially less favourable [review for America](https://www.americamagazine.org/arts-culture/2024/09/24/review-intermezzo-rooney-rubsam-248862/), Robert Rubsam argues that too much of the significant conflict belongs to the characters' pasts, leaving their present encounters insufficiently dramatic. He is particularly dissatisfied with the space afforded Sylvia's independent life.

The disagreement matters more than a score. A mind returning to an old hurt can be the substance of a novel, or it can become a substitute for present action. Which is happening may vary from scene to scene. A reader does not have to take a permanent side before opening the book.

The question about the women deserves similar care. A character without an independent viewpoint can still have a vivid life. Equally, a novel about understanding people has not automatically understood everyone it contains. When Sylvia or Naomi appears, how much can we discover about her own concerns? How much of what we hear remains organised around Peter's need for her?

This is a question to carry into the full novel, rather than a verdict drawn from a sample. It also asks something of our appetite as readers. We may want a woman to comfort a man, tell him the truth, or finally make him change. She can do any of those things and still have a day to live after leaving his company. Are we curious about that day?

## The suit was easy

Peter can remember what Ivan wore. Remembering does not tell him what to ask.

That seems a useful place to leave the introduction, with a difficulty smaller than the grand question of whether love can save us. Once we have known someone for years, can we still hear information that does not fit? Can an older brother allow the younger one to have changed without asking him to demonstrate it according to the family's established rules?

Those questions need not lead to limitless patience. A person can be misunderstood and still behave badly; understanding more does not cancel the effects of what he does. It may, however, change the conversation we are able to have with him. The familiar explanation loses some of its authority. Another question becomes possible.

Start with Peter if you want to hear a confident voice giving itself away. Start with Ivan and Margaret if you want to sit inside the uncertainty of an encounter before anyone knows what it will become. The two extracts offer enough to discover whether you want to stay.

Their father is gone. There are still messages to answer, people to see, words that came out wrongly. Peter has a brother whose suit he can describe and whose days he has not yet learned to ask about.
zh_body:
父亲的葬礼已经结束，Peter还记得弟弟穿的那身不合适的西装。他对Ivan的衣着、神态和不自在都很有看法，仿佛这个年轻人从头到脚都需要哥哥帮忙收拾。然而，当Naomi问起弟弟怎么样，他却承认自己其实不知道。这个小小的落差，出现在[出版社公开的开篇试读](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374602635/intermezzo/)里。

一个人可以对弟弟如此熟悉，又对他正在经历的事情如此陌生。对还没有读过《Intermezzo》的人来说，这或许是比任何主题概括都更好的入口：先认识这一对不太懂得彼此的兄弟，看看他们怎样把亲近、烦躁、优越感和牵挂混在同一句话里。

这是爱尔兰作家Sally Rooney的第四部长篇小说，出版于2024年。即使没有读过她的《正常人》，也完全可以从这里开始。故事围绕父亲去世后的Peter和Ivan，以及与他们发生亲密关系的三位女性展开，主要生活空间落在都柏林和爱尔兰小镇。人物关系很快就能辨认，进入他们的内心却需要更多时间。

它的吸引力也从这种时间差中生长出来。读者可能已经对一个人的言行作出了判断，下一段文字才让我们听见他没有说出口的迟疑。阅读于是多了一点不安：方才那个看起来很容易理解的人，似乎又需要重新认识了。

## 两个兄弟，各自以为对方比较容易生活

Peter三十二岁，是都柏林的一名律师；Ivan二十二岁，是参加比赛的国际象棋棋手。哥哥擅长与人打交道，弟弟更习惯可以仔细推演的世界。两人相差十岁，这个距离使他们对彼此的认识带着一种家庭内部特有的惯性：哥哥容易继续看见那个尚未长大的孩子，弟弟则把哥哥当成已经掌握成人生活规则的人。

有趣的是，这两种想象都能找到表面证据。一个人的工作、衣着、说话方式，足以让另一个人推断他过得怎么样。尤其在家人之间，这些推断很容易获得无需核查的权威：我看着你长大，难道还不了解你？小说给读者的便利，恰恰是能够越过这样的熟悉，分别靠近两个人。

Peter的体面已经不能保证他安稳入睡，父亲去世后，他依靠药物帮助自己休息。Ivan则远没有“棋坛天才”这个称呼听起来那么确定。在[与Cressida Leyshon的访谈](https://www.newyorker.com/books/this-week-in-fiction/sally-rooney-07-08-24)中，Rooney提醒读者，他有才能，却不是世界冠军级的人物。对他来说，如何评价自己、如何与别人相处，都还没有现成答案。

因此，读这本书不需要先懂国际象棋。知道棋手也会面对失去方向的生活，就足够了。我们很容易相信，一个人在某件事上足够聪明，就应该也能把自己安排妥当；小说把两个聪明人放在同一场丧失之后，让这种期待渐渐显出它的苛刻。

丧亲提供了故事的共同起点，却没有给兄弟一套共同的语言。Peter的镇定可能让人误以为他不需要帮助，Ivan的不善表达也可能被看成没有什么可说。初读时，值得暂缓对两个人的排名。谁更成熟、谁更真诚，当然可以讨论，但阅读的乐趣往往发生在排名失效的地方：一个惹人厌烦的人忽然变得可以理解，而一个让人怜惜的人也会说出伤人的话。

## 爱情并不等人把生活整理好

与兄弟关系同时展开的，是几段已经带着过去的爱情。Peter与昔日恋人Sylvia保持着深厚牵连；Sylvia因一次意外长期承受身体疼痛。他又与年轻的大学生Naomi交往，经济上的不对等也进入两人的关系。弟弟这一边，Ivan在一场棋艺活动中结识了年长的Margaret，她在当地艺术中心工作，也正处在自己婚姻的困难之中。

Peter和Naomi的关系，从开篇就有一种难以归类的亲近：他愿意在经济上帮助她，她却直到这次见面才知道他的父亲去世了。两个人已经如此靠近，重要的消息却没有抵达对方那里。

这样的细节使恋爱关系不再只是人物介绍中的一条连线。一个人可以在某些方面允许另一个人进入，另一些地方却仍关着门；也可能双方都没有明确决定过，门就一直关在那里。钱、身体、家庭消息，各自以不同的速度进入亲密。读Peter这条线时，可以留意这些速度差：他的困境有一部分已经在日常相处中发生，连他自己也未必及时察觉。

Ivan与Margaret的初遇尤其适合作为试读。她误以为来参加活动的棋坛神童是个小孩子，面对已经站在眼前的Ivan，才发现自己弄错了。这个带着喜剧感的认识过程，收在公开节选[《Opening Theory》](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2024/07/08/opening-theory-fiction-sally-rooney)中。

Ivan很想继续与Margaret交谈，同时又担心把她工作中的友善误认成私人的好感。吸引力刚刚出现，他已经开始检查自己的反应。

这点窘迫让他的安静有了可亲的内容。从外面看，一个人似乎只是没有接上话；进入他的意识，才发现那几秒钟里已经经过许多斟酌。Margaret的工作要求她接待来访者，Ivan又确实被她吸引，普通的礼貌因此多了一层不确定的意味。棋盘之外，他还要学着辨认一种无法预先算好的回应。

三位女性的存在也使小说不只围绕兄弟之间的竞争旋转。她们与两人的年龄差、生活经验和物质条件各不相同，同一件事落在不同的人身上，重量便会变化。听一个男人解释自己的感情时，最好也留意他解释中的女人：她的担忧是否被听见，她所承担的代价是否被说清，都是值得自己读下去的部分。

年龄差又使两条恋爱线彼此映照。哥哥与年轻的大学生相处，弟弟则被一位年长女性吸引；把这两个情形放在一起，人们习惯的判断标准便容易浮现。经济能力、生活经验和性别期待，会怎样影响我们对一段关系的看法？即使双方都已成年，年龄的意义也没有就此消失。这里有爱情故事的吸引力，也有足以使人意见不一的现实质地。

## 这本书的速度，在句子里面

选择《Intermezzo》之前，最好知道它会要求怎样的阅读耐心。它把许多篇幅交给人物意识的运动，读者需要留意刚才的想法怎样在下一刻发生变化。公开的Peter开篇已经显示出这种写法：句子经常短促地停下，念头之间快速切换，观察、判断和记忆紧挨在一起，未必先替读者整理成顺畅的说明。

这种声音初读可能有些费力。我们习惯小说先把情境布置清楚，再告诉我们人物怎样反应；这里却常常像在一个人已经开始思考之后，才走进他的脑海。理解稍微落后于句子，也是体验的一部分。Peter越急着判断，读者越有可能感觉到，语言的流利并不总能带来内心的安稳。

在[ABC的评论](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-10-01/intermezzo-sally-rooney-review/104413414)中，Rosie Ofori Ward注意到，Peter的段落更破碎，Ivan的思绪则倾向于较完整、审慎的展开。Margaret也拥有自己的内在视角。同是贴近人物内心的第三人称叙述，进入不同人物时，句子的节奏也随之改变。

这种变化值得慢慢熟悉。同一个动作，在旁观者眼里可能已经明确，回到行动者的意识里却仍充满试探。读一会儿之后，我们留意的可能不再只是对话内容，还包括一个人如何准备那句话，以及说出以后怎样在心里修改它。这也是亲密关系小说能够把很小的事件写得紧张的原因。

Rooney在这里继续采用不以引号框住对话的写法，人物说出的话与叙述、内心活动之间有时相当贴近。[Associated Press的Curtis Yee](https://apnews.com/article/7bd20450504ea13131f770a4bac9d33b)尤其欣赏小说捕捉尚未清楚成形的情绪的能力。

如果读英文时偶尔需要回看一句，确认那是说出口的话还是一个念头，不必急着怀疑自己的理解。可以先读完一个场景，再回头看声音怎样移动。对喜欢语言和心理细节的人来说，这种小小的辨认工作可能很有吸引力；如果你目前希望读一部事件密集、转折迅速的小说，最好先试读，感受一下这个节奏是否适合自己。

## 赞赏之外，也有值得带进阅读的分歧

Ward欣赏小说更慢、更深入的写法，同时指出Sylvia与Naomi的形象受到Peter视角的限制。

[America的Robert Rubsam](https://www.americamagazine.org/arts-culture/2024/09/24/review-intermezzo-rooney-rubsam-248862/)则更不满意。他肯定部分城市描写、谈话与幽默，却认为人物的重要冲突过多地发生在小说展开之前，当下行动有时不足以支撑作品的思想分量。他也质疑Sylvia的独立生活是否得到了充分呈现。

这两种反应不必提前裁定。对一些读者而言，思想反复经过同一个伤口，正是阅读的意义；对另一些读者而言，过多的反复会削弱人物行动的力量。是否喜欢这本小说，可能就与这种偏好有关。只把它介绍成感情细腻，容易让人忽略它的阅读负担；只强调缓慢，又会错过细小心理变化可能带来的强烈感受。

配角的问题同样值得保留。一个人物没有获得独立视角，未必就没有自己的生命；但也不能因为作品关心爱与理解，便预先相信每个人都得到了充分理解。读者可以特别留意Sylvia和Naomi出现时的谈话：这些场景让我们认识了她们多少，又有多少仍是Peter的需要和想象？这样的观察不会破坏故事，反而让阅读多了一条可以自己判断的线索。

## 西装记得，日子却不知道

再想起开头那个对弟弟的西装很有看法、却说不清弟弟过得怎样的Peter。一个人总还有一些生活，没有被亲近者对他的描述说完。哥哥的眼光不能替弟弟说明一切，弟弟眼中的成熟也无法替哥哥安顿悲伤。读者同样可能把刚刚形成的印象，误当成已经认识了这个人。

我们也可以留意自己对配角的期待。当我们盼着某个人使主角得到安慰、重新振作，或者终于作出正确选择时，她离开这个房间以后的生活呢？她还要面对谁，完成什么，又希望有谁问问她过得如何？小说有没有让我们看见，是一个值得带进全书的问题。

重新认识一个人，并不意味着替他的一切行为找到借口。Peter可能有他的痛苦，同时仍会伤人。Ivan值得被听见，也不必因此成为每次争执里更正确的那一个。多知道一点，有时只是让原来那句说得太顺的话停下来，容得下一次真正的询问。

可以从英文开篇或《Opening Theory》试起。前者让你靠近Peter的声音，后者提供另一种相遇的节奏。如果读完后，你开始惦记这个哥哥为什么如此疲惫，那个弟弟与Margaret下一次见面会怎样，那么继续读下去的理由已经足够。

父亲已经不在。Peter还记得那身西装，只是弟弟最近怎样过日子，他还没有好好问过。
en_source_note: This introduction draws on the publisher's public opening extract, the published excerpt “Opening Theory,” Sally Rooney's interview, and the signed reviews linked below. Close reading focuses on those extracts; comments on the full novel are attributed to the reviewers. The reading questions and interpretations are our own.
